newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone capital calmer, U.S, UK condemn coup.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone capital calmer, U.S, UK condemn coup.

text.p: Shooting died down in Sierra Leone's capital on Tuesday, two days after a coup ousted the elected civilian government, but the international community kept up its chorus of condemnation.
The Armed Forces Revolutionary Council, in a statement broadcast on national radio, promised to cooperate with any evacuation effort for foreign nationals.

The United States called for restoration of the civilian government of President Ahmed Tejan Kabbah, elected little more than a year ago. The United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity have also condemned the coup.
Former colonial power Britain, which on Monday limited itself to expressing concern that British property had been looted, on Tuesday deplored the coup and the level of accompanying violence.
Shops, banks, schools and markets remained closed on Tuesday despite the coup leaders' appeals to people to return to work. Only a few roadside traders ventured out.
The United Nations World Food programme said looters had taken 1,650 tonnes of food aid, 15 vehicles and other equipment from its Freetown warehouses.
"The United States condemns the coup which overthrew Sierra Leone's first democratically elected government in three decades," the U.S. State Department said.
Prominent businessman and diamond dealer Jamil Sahid Mohamed said his son Hassan had been shot dead by unidentified men in military uniforms who broke into his house.

The new military leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah was among those freed when soldiers broke into Freetown's Pademba Road jail early on Sunday. He was accused of planning a coup and had been due to appear in court the following day.
He is a northern Limba, the same ethnic group as former president Joseph Momoh, who was ousted in a coup in 1992 and lives in exile in neighbouring Guinea, where Kabbah also arrived on Sunday.
Many northerners resented what they saw as domination of the civilian government by southern Mendes like Kabbah, but the coup does not appear to have wide public support in Freetown.

Kabbah told the BBC he was still the legitimate president. "I am sad and angry because I am a Sierra Leonean and I see and I hear and I know that a group of hooligans are destroying my country," he said.
The coup leaders said they wanted to bring rebels of the Revolutionary United Front into the government to consolidate an elusive peace in the country's civil war.
Troops searched houses on Monday looking for ministers of the former civilian government, and military sources said five former ministers were detained at the military headquarters.
In neighbouring Liberia, the ECOMOG West African peacekeeping force sealed the land border with Sierra Leone on Monday and its naval units mounted coastal patrols.
The deployments fuelled speculation that the Nigerian-led force was about to intervene in Sierra Leone where its troops were drawn into fighting at the presidential offices on Sunday.
Port officials and military sources in Monrovia said two naval boats left with hundreds of battle-ready peacekeeping troops on Sunday night, presumably heading for Sierra Leone.
Staff at Freetown's main hospital said at least 18 people were killed in Sunday's fighting.
